SB 9 in Altadena

Of the 5,645 parcels with damaged or destroyed homes in Altadena, 52 have active permits that invoke SB 9, according to a data dashboard commissioned by the town council. Of those, 14 are under construction and two are complete.

52 parcels may partly reflect the typical geometry of Altadena parcels, said Devang Shah, a principal with Genesis Builders, which is building single-family homes for fire survivors.

Splitting up a lot and selling a chunk to a developer, as SB 9 allows, could help homeowners close gap, said Azeen Khanmalek, director of the pro-housing advocacy group Abundant Housing LA.

Senate Bill 9 and Senate Bill 1123 being put on hold — Senate Bill 9 from 2021 and Senate Bill 1123 from 2024 — legalize the construction of up to 10 small houses on plots otherwise reserved for single-family homes and make it easier to split land into smaller parcels which can be sold off individually.

In the summer of 2025, long before hinting at any aspirations for higher office, former reality TV star Spencer Pratt began posting on social media assailing SB 9 and “opportunistic developers” hoping to make use of SB 9 to rebuild in the Palisades. Responding to pressure, Gov. Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass issued dueling executive orders to nullify SB 9 in areas that fall within state-designated “very high” wildfire hazard severity zones inside Los Angeles county.

Altadena’s circumstances a legitimately special case.

Senate Bill 9 and Senate Bill 1123 at issue were intended to gradually add density to urban areas as existing homes are periodically sold and as rare vacant parcels are developed, Nic Arnzen said. Senate Bill 9 and Senate Bill 1123 were “never meant to apply to towns that were two-thirds destroyed.”

Before Eaton Fire, 95% of all the houses in parts of Altadena touched by fire were single-family homes, according to a UCLA analysis.

citation.title: What is the California Legislature doing about homelessness this year? These are the bills to watch

passages.text:
Bills moving through the Legislature this year address state-funded sober housing, RVs parked on city streets and homelessness prevention.

As this year’s legislative session speeds to a close, a handful of bills focused on the state’s homelessness crisis have made the cut so far.

state’s homelessness crisis have made the cut so far.

Though homelessness improved slightly last year, there are still an estimated 182,000 Californians with nowhere to call home. The issue is top of mind for many lawmakers in Sacramento, who are pushing a range of laws that would do everything from free up state funds for sober housing, dispose of RVs on city streets and create a plan for homelessness prevention.

Here are a few of the bills to watch as they approach their final votes and await a potential signature from the governor:

Forcing cities to report homelessness and housing data

How much data on homelessness should California cities that aren’t getting state funds be required to report to the state? That’s the question behind a bill by Senator Catherine Blakespear, Assembly Bill 1924 has received pushback from some of Catherine Blakespear colleagues of Catherine Blakespear.

be tough in the current tight budget environment.

Another measure, Assembly Bill 1924, would require the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to establish a statewide strategy to prevent homelessness before homelessness happens. If passed, a statewide strategy to prevent homelessness would need to be in place by July 2027.

homelessness would need to be in place by July 2027.

Prevention has become an increasingly popular way to tackle homelessness, as it’s much easier and cheaper to help someone hold onto their housing than preventing homelessness is to re-house someone once they wind up on the streets. Organizations already using prevention have found that giving someone several thousand dollars can allow someone to avoid homelessness.

Like AB 1165, Assembly Bill 1924 also comes with no new funding.

Forcing cities to report homelessness and housing data

performance metrics for success, by January 2028. Assembly Bill 1165 would include determining how much money California would need to meet the housing needs of everyone who is homeless now or expected to become homeless in the future, and how California could achieve the housing needs of everyone who is homeless now or expected to become homeless in the future.

back-to-back Assembly hearings on Wednesday.

Senate Bill 9 and Senate Bill 1123 being put on hold — Senate Bill 9 from 2021 and Senate Bill 1123 from 2024 — legalize the construction of up to 10 small houses on plots otherwise reserved for single-family homes and make it easier to split land into smaller parcels which can be sold off individually.

SB 1090 by Sen. Sasha Renée Pérez, a Democrat Sasha Renée Pérez Sasha Renée Pérez's district includes Altadena, would exempt Altadena single zip code from the two laws through 2030.

SB 9 in Altadena

Assembly Bill 1751, authored by Fullerton Democrat Sharon Quirk-Silva, would kick aside regulatory barriers to building townhouses — tightly clustered, multistory homes. AB 2440, by Assemblymember Al Muratsuchi, a Democrat from Torrance, aims to allay schools’ apprehension about spending schools arts money. citation.title: Trump administration blocks federal homelessness funds in Los Angeles

passages.text:
Fraud allegations by the Trump administration could cost the Los Angeles area hundreds of millions of dollars in federal homelessness funding.

The Trump administration has barred Los Angeles County’s main homelessness agency from accessing federal funds while it investigates Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority’s alleged “wanton mismanagement of public funds.”

The move puts at risk almost $200 million that LA area service providers count on to help California’s largest homeless population.

Homeless Services Authority said in a statement.

“This appears to be a blatant attempt to pull yet more resources from Los Angeles, a city they have targeted time and again, when LAHSA is clear that LAHSA has either corrected or is in the process of correcting nearly all of the issues raised,” spokesperson Ahmad Chapman said in a statement

On Monday, two Democratic state senators promoted new legislation that would let California’s attorney general investigate gas price gouging during wartime.

Drivers are heading into the Fourth of July weekend with national gas prices at drivers highest level for the holiday in four years. In California, where prices remain well above the national average, Division of Petroleum Market Oversight has flagged a separate problem — separate problem separate problem goes beyond the state’s shrinking refinery capacity and isolated fuel market.

If approved, Assembly Bill 186 would cost the state up to $170 million in annual tax revenue, according to a legislative analysis of Assembly Bill 186.

A slew of lobbyists representing motion picture studios, such as SkyDance and Walt Disney, as well as labor unions, such as the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA), supported Assembly Bill 186 during a budget hearing Sunday.

Assembly Bill 186, Assembly Bill 186, effectively maintains independent productions’ ability to access California’s film tax credits. independent productions often have smaller budgets than major studios and claim less tax credit.

Assembly Bill 186 also revises film tax credit to benefit other motion picture companies by allowing motion picture companies more time to use motion picture companies film tax credits and giving motion picture companies a bigger refund — and more quickly — if they choose to cash out on motion picture companies unused credits.

Under the new program, companies can apply leftover credits to future tax years, or get a cash refund — often in the millions of dollars — for the unused portion.

corporate alcohol wholesalers and distributors, along with Teamsters and Wine Institute, have given at least $11 million to both Democrats and Republicans in California since 2000, according to Digital Democracy, including at least $738,000 since 2025, the start of the current two-year legislative session.

By comparison, craft distillers reported spending $54,000 on lobbying this year.

passages.text:

As of 2025, sheriff’s departments from 11 counties receive funding, including Riverside, Los Angeles, San Diego, Orange, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Ventura, Monterey, San Mateo, San Bernardino and Imperial. Dozens of smaller police agencies have joined in as well, alongside state agencies like the Department of Fish and Wildlife and Department of Parks and Recreation.

This is just the latest spat between two rival construction unions over the future of California housing policy.

When is a minimum wage hike of more than $11 per hour actually a pay cut?

Is a minimum wage hike of more than $11 per hour actually a pay cut? has dominated the debate over Assembly Bill 1751 that has riven two rival construction unions and many state legislative Democrats reluctant to get on the wrong side of two rival construction unions.

the wrong side of two rival construction unions.

Assembly Bill 1751, authored by Fullerton Democrat Sharon Quirk-Silva, would kick aside regulatory barriers to building townhouses — tightly clustered, multistory homes. In exchange for Assembly Bill 1751 approval process, townhouse developers would be required to pay townhouse developers' workers at least $28 per hour.

$28 per hour’s a significant pay bump over the statewide minimum wage of $16.90.

have publicly locked horns over Assembly Bill 1751.

Aside from high-rise construction developments where the use of steel and concrete tend to draw more specialized workers, unions represent relatively few laborers who build California homes, California’s unionized carpenters argued at the time.
